evaluationProducerReferences.content: Offensive language: The GermEval BIBREF11 shared task focused on Offensive language identification in German tweets.

facets.topic: focused on Offensive language identification

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Untargeted (UNT): Posts containing non-targeted profanity and swearing. Posts with general profanity are not targeted, but they contain non-acceptable language.

facets.topic: Posts containing non-targeted profanity and swearing

evaluationProducerReferences.content: A dataset of over 8,500 annotated tweets was provided for a course-grained binary classification task in which systems were trained to discriminate between offensive and non-offensive tweets and a second task where the organizers broke down the offensive class into three classes: profanity, insult, and abuse.

facets.topic: A dataset of over 8,500 annotated tweets

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Most prior work focuses on a different aspect of offensive language such as abusive language BIBREF0 , BIBREF1 , (cyber-)aggression BIBREF2 , (cyber-)bullying BIBREF3 , BIBREF4 , toxic comments INLINEFORM0 , hate speech BIBREF5 , BIBREF6 , BIBREF7 , BIBREF8 , BIBREF9 , BIBREF10 , and offensive language BIBREF11 .

facets.topic: focuses on a different aspect of offensive language

evaluationProducerReferences.content: In the OLID dataset, we use a hierarchical annotation model split into three levels to distinguish between whether language is offensive or not (A), and type (B) and target (C) of the offensive language.

facets.topic: hierarchical annotation model split into three levels

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Different abusive and offense language identification sub-tasks have been explored in the past few years including aggression identification, bullying detection, hate speech, toxic comments, and offensive language.

facets.topic: abusive and offense language identification sub-tasks

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Different abusive and offense language identification sub-tasks have been explored in the past few years including aggression identification, bullying detection, hate speech, toxic comments, and offensive language.

facets.entity: Different abusive and offense language identification sub-tasks
facets.topic: have been explored in the past few years

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Prior work has focused on these aspects of offensive language in Twitter BIBREF3 , BIBREF7 , BIBREF8 , BIBREF11 , Wikipedia comments, and Facebook posts BIBREF2 .

facets.topic: has focused on these aspects of offensive language

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Hate speech identification: It is perhaps the most widespread abusive language detection sub-task.

facets.topic: Hate speech identification

evaluationProducerReferences.content: There have been several studies published on this sub-task such as kwok2013locate and djuric2015hate who build a binary classifier to distinguish between `clean' comments and comments containing hate speech and profanity.

facets.topic: build a binary classifier

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Wiegand et al. ( BIBREF11 ) followed this trend as well on German tweets. In their evaluation, they have a task to detect offensive vs not offensive tweets and a second task for distinguishing between the offensive tweets as profanity, insult, or abuse.

facets.topic: followed this trend as well on German tweets

evaluationProducerReferences.content: However, no prior work has explored the target of the offensive language, which is important in many scenarios, e.g., when studying hate speech with respect to a specific target.

conditions: when studying hate speech with respect to a specific target
facets.topic: has explored the target of the offensive language

evaluationProducerReferences.content: More recently, Davidson et al. davidson2017automated presented the hate speech detection dataset containing over 24,000 English tweets labeled as non offensive, hate speech, and profanity.

facets.topic: presented the hate speech detection dataset

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Recently, Waseem et. al. ( BIBREF12 ) acknowledged the similarities among prior work and discussed the need for a typology that differentiates between whether the (abusive) language is directed towards a specific individual or entity or towards a generalized group and whether the abusive content is explicit or implicit.

facets.topic: discussed the need for a typology

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Level A discriminates between offensive (OFF) and non-offensive (NOT) tweets.

facets.topic: discriminates between offensive (OFF) and non-offensive (NOT) tweets

evaluationProducerReferences.content: One of the most common strategies to tackle the problem is to train systems capable of recognizing offensive content, which then can be deleted or set aside for human moderation.

facets.topic: train systems capable of recognizing offensive content

evaluationProducerReferences.content: This paper presents OLID, a new dataset with annotation of type and target of offensive language. OLID is the official dataset of the shared task SemEval 2019 Task 6: Identifying and Categorizing Offensive Language in Social Media (OffensEval) BIBREF16 .

facets.topic: official dataset of the shared task SemEval 2019 Task 6

evaluationProducerReferences.content: In OffensEval, each annotation level in OLID is an independent sub-task. The dataset contains 14,100 tweets and is released freely to the research community.

facets.topic: contains 14,100 tweets

evaluationProducerReferences.content: We present baseline experiments using SVMs and neural networks to identify the offensive tweets, discriminate between insults, threats, and profanity, and finally to identify the target of the offensive messages. The results show that this is a challenging task. A CNN-based sentence classifier achieved the best results in all three sub-tasks.

facets.topic: achieved the best results in all three sub-tasks

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Offensive (OFF): We label a post as offensive if it contains any form of non-acceptable language (profanity) or a targeted offense, which can be veiled or direct. This category includes insults, threats, and posts containing profane language or swear words.

conditions: if it contains any form of non-acceptable language (profanity) or a targeted offense, which can be veiled or direct
facets.topic: We label a post as offensive if it contains any form of non-acceptable language (profanity) or a targeted offense

evaluationProducerReferences.content: One of them is the one by xu2012learning which apply sentiment analysis to detect bullying in tweets. xu2012learning use topic models to to identify relevant topics in bullying.

facets.topic: apply sentiment analysis to detect bullying in tweets

evaluationProducerReferences.content: Toxic comments: The Toxic Comment Classification Challenge was an open competition at Kaggle which provided participants with comments from Wikipedia labeled in six classes: toxic, severe toxic, obscene, threat, insult, identity hate.

facets.topic: was an open competition at Kaggle

evaluationProducerReferences.content: First, unlike the two other classes, OTH is a heterogeneous collection of targets. It includes offensive tweets targeted at organizations, situations, events, etc. making it more challenging for systems to learn discriminative properties of this class.

facets.topic: heterogeneous collection of targets

questions.question: How is the sequential nature of the story captured?

result.answer:
The encoder takes the images in order, one at every timestep t, using Inception v3 to obtain each image's representation. [1]
An LSTM summarizes the sequence of images; at time t=5 it has encoded the 5 images and provides the sequence's context through its last hidden state h_e^(t). [2][3]
The model contains five independent decoders, one for each image in the sequence; all use the encoder's last hidden state as their first hidden state and the corresponding image embedding as their first input. [4]
Each decoder generates a sequence of words for its image, and the final story is the concatenation of the outputs of the 5 decoders. [5]
The first decoder generates words for the first image, the second for the second image, and so on, allowing each decoder to learn a specific language model for each position of the sequence. [6]
For instance, the first decoder learns the opening sentences of the story while the last decoder learns the closing sentences. [7]

result.answer:
模型先用LSTM编码器按时间步依次输入5张图像，在t=5时以最后隐藏状态h_e^(t)作为整段序列的上下文。 [1][2][3]
模型包含5个独立解码器，每个解码器对应序列中的一张图像，分别生成该位置的词序列，最终故事由5个解码器的输出拼接而成。 [4][5][6]
每个解码器以编码器最后隐藏状态（上下文）初始化，并以对应图像嵌入e(I_i)作为首个输入。 [7][4]
这种按位置分配解码器的设计使每个解码器学习序列特定位置的语言模型，例如第一个解码器学习故事开头、最后一个学习结尾。 [6][8]

result.answer:
No. Adding word alignments in parallel sentences yields only small, non-significant improvements, even when some labeled data is available in the source language. [1]
The results indicate that little information about semantic roles can be learned from this parallel data setup. [2]

documents.title: GlossBERT: BERT for Word Sense Disambiguation with Gloss Knowledge

questions.question: How does the neural network architecture accomodate an unknown amount of senses per word?

result.answer:
GlossBERT treats WSD as a sentence-pair classification problem: it constructs context-gloss pairs from the glosses of all possible senses (in WordNet) of the target word. [1]
For each target, its candidate senses come from entries of its lemma in a pre-defined sense inventory (usually WordNet), so the number of candidate senses is not fixed in advance. [2]
GlossBERT 将 WSD 视为句对分类问题：它用目标词在 WordNet 中所有可能义项的释义构造 context-gloss 对。 [1][3]
模型以 context-gloss 对为输入，取首个 token [CLS] 的最终隐状态作为整个序列的表示，并加一个二分类层（label∈{yes, no}）。 [4]
测试时，模型输出每个 context-gloss 对 label=yes 的概率，并选择概率最高的义项作为目标词的预测标签。 [5]
每个目标词有 N 个 context-gloss 对训练实例（label∈{yes, no}）。 [6]

questions.question: Why masking words in the decoder is helpful?

result.answer:
掩码解码器中的词有助于利用BERT等上下文语言模型的能力：refine解码过程提供更完整的输入序列，与其预训练过程一致。 [1]
设计词级refine解码器是因为该过程类似BERT预训练中的完形填空任务，从而能借助上下文语言模型生成更流畅自然的序列。 [2]
refine过程的主要目的是用BERT的上下文化表示增强解码器。 [3]
在第二阶段，对摘要中的每个词进行掩码，并用refine解码器逐个预测精炼后的词。 [4]
refine解码器以生成的摘要草稿为输入，输出精炼后的摘要，并基于源文档及其他词一次聚焦一个词。 [5][6]

掩码词级精炼解码器之所以有帮助，是因为该过程类似于BERT预训练中的完形填空任务，借助上下文语言模型的能力，解码器可以生成更流畅、更自然的序列。 [1]

该模型基于BERT，在编码器和解码器过程中利用预训练语言模型，并且可以端到端训练，无需手工特征。 [1]
训练时模型目标是两个过程目标之和，使用“teacher-forcing”算法联合训练；训练中把真实摘要输入每个解码器并最小化目标。 [2]
模型目标函数为 L_model = L̂_dec + L̂_refine。 [3]
模型变体包括：One-Stage（基于BERT、带复制机制的序列到序列模型）、Two-Stage（在One-Stage上增加word-refine解码器）、Two-Stage + RL（带refine过程并结合RL目标的完整模型）。 [4]

documents.title: A Hybrid Architecture for Multi-Party Conversational Systems

questions.question: What is the state of the art described in the paper?

result.answer:
The paper reviews the state of the art on conversational systems from three perspectives: types of interactions, types of architecture, and types of context reasoning, and consolidates them in a comparison table. [1]
In the reviewed state of the art, most proposed approaches for context reasoning rely on rules using logics and knowledge bases. [2]
The most recent state of the art for developing such systems has employed Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Dynamic Context-Sensitive Generation, and Memory Networks, among others. [3]
Sukhbaatar's work presents the state of the art of recent efforts to capture dialogue context as long-term structure within sequences using RNNs or LSTM-based models. [4]
Among the reviewed systems, ELIZA was one of the first software programs created to understand natural language processing, built by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT in 1966 and known for acting like a psychotherapist. [5]
ELIZA was created to tackle five fundamental technical problems: identifying critical words, discovering a minimal context, choosing appropriate transformations, generating appropriate responses, and providing an ending capacity for ELIZA scripts. [6]
PARRY was developed by Kenneth Colby, a psychiatrist at Stanford University, in the early 1970s. [7]
A.L.I.C.E. appeared in 1995, and its current version uses AIML, an XML language designed for creating stimulus-response chat robots. [8]
Cleverbot (1997-2014) is a chatbot developed by the British AI scientist Rollo Carpenter. [9]
The paper states that most existing chatbots, from ELIZA to modern state-of-the-art ones, fall into this category. [10]
The paper notes a lack of methods and tools to design and engineer coordination and mediation among chatbots and humans, and a lack of research on building coordination laws integrated with natural language for chatbot engines. [11][12]
The authors state that, to the best of their knowledge, the architecture proposed in the paper is the first in the state of the art designed to support coordinated aware chatbots in a multiparty conversation. [13]

The paper states that most existing chatbots, from ELIZA to modern state-of-the-art ones, fall into this category.

The paper notes a lack of methods and tools to design and engineer coordination and mediation among chatbots and humans, and a lack of research on building coordination laws integrated with natural language for chatbot engines.

The authors state that, to the best of their knowledge, the architecture proposed in the paper is the first in the state of the art designed to support coordinated aware chatbots in a multiparty conversation.

论文从交互类型、架构类型和上下文推理类型三个视角讨论对话系统的研究现状，并用一张表汇总比较。 [1]
ELIZA 是最早用于理解自然语言处理的软件之一，由 Joseph Weizenbaum 于 1966 年在 MIT 创建，以扮演心理治疗师著称。 [2]
ELIZA 旨在解决五个“基本技术问题”：识别关键词、发现最小上下文、选择适当变换、生成适当响应，以及为 ELIZA 脚本提供结束能力。 [3]
ELIZA 之后出现 PARRY，由斯坦福大学精神病学家 Kenneth Colby 在 1970 年代初开发。 [4]
A.L.I.C.E. 出现于 1995 年，其当前版本使用为创建刺激-响应聊天机器人而设计的 XML 语言 AIML。 [5]
Cleverbot（1997-2014）是由英国 AI 科学家 Rollo Carpenter 开发的聊天机器人。 [6]
在上下文推理方面，现有大多数方法依赖使用逻辑和知识库的规则。 [7]
近期开发此类系统的最新研究采用了循环神经网络（RNN）、动态上下文敏感生成和记忆网络等。 [8]
